paras: The Prairie Ridge mock hanging was a staged lynching on a Thursday night in early January 1881, about three miles west of Prairie Ridge in Saline County, Missouri, carried out by a masked band by arrangement with Sheriff John Cason. The band pretended to hang a willing participant, Jasper Smith, then put a rope around the neck of Thos. Barnes, a prisoner accused of burglary, until he confessed; no one was hurt.

Barnes, a traveling photographer working from a tent at Prairie Ridge, was accused of taking $150 and a revolver from Frank M. Stotts's store and was arrested after being traced by tracks in the snow. Although "there was no positive proof against Barnes," Sam Cockrell, E. B. Ruckle and about twenty-five others formed a band and agreed with the sheriff to ambush his party on the road to Marshall.

When the sheriff's party met the masked men, Smith, strapped under the arms, was suspended for four or five minutes while Barnes watched from about thirty yards away, then "pronounced dead" and cut down unhurt. The band seized Barnes, placed a rope around his neck and told him he too must die. He first named Jasper Smith and a Joseph Smith as accomplices and led guards back to Prairie Ridge, where part of the money and the revolver were recovered. Told of the ruse, he said he alone was guilty and was returned to the sheriff.
Barnes was jailed at Marshall on Friday to await sentencing at the next term of court; no action against the masked men and no report of his trial appear in the coverage.

The only known account ran in the Sedalia Weekly Bazoo of January 11, 1881, based on a story Stotts told the paper. Headlined "Barnes' Bad Break" with the deck "His Crookedness Causes Him to be Strung Up by a Masked Mob," it called the band "among the best of Saline's citizens" and the scheme "a novel plan." The paper treated Barnes's guilt as settled, said he "will now suffer the penalty of his crime," and gave no race for anyone involved.

bases: A masked band, by prior arrangement with the sheriff, staged a hanging of a willing participant and then put a rope around the neck of a prisoner accused of burglary, threatening him with death until he confessed; no one was hurt (A1).

About twenty-five or more masked men threatened Thos. Barnes with hanging to extract a confession to burglary, but no one was killed; the man they pretended to hang, Jasper Smith, was in on the plan and was not hurt (A1).
Only one report was found, the Sedalia Weekly Bazoo's retelling of an account given by the burglary victim, Frank M. Stotts (A1).
